newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China flags fly briefly over Japan-held islands.
newsitem.headline: China flags fly briefly over Japan-held islands.

text.p: Taiwan and Hong Kong activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon on Monday, swam ashore and hoisted Chinese flags on a deserted East China Sea archipelago in a challenge to Japan's claim of sovereignty.

Four activists put ashore at dawn by a protest flotilla raised the red five-star flag of the communist People's Republic of China and blue-and-red banner of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China, Taiwan and Hong Kong media reported from the scene.

"Everyone aboard the boats offshore let up a great cheer when they saw the flags," a Taiwan state radio reporter said by ship-to-shore radio from one of 50 protest boats from Taiwan carrying about 300 activists.
Japanese maritime police, whose force of some 30 vessels and several helicopters failed to thwart the landing, swiftly put officers ashore to remove the flags, the reports said.
Hong Kong radio said two demonstrators had fallen into the sea from one of the protest boats and were rescued by fellow activists.
Kyodo put the number of successful landings at two, saying each craft put four people ashore for 10 to 20 minutes.
Japan's Maritime Safety Agency confirmed that protesters had landed and soon returned to their ships.
The protesters' command ship ordered the private flotilla to withdraw to 12 nautical miles from the islands, reports said.
Protest leaders pledged to land on the islands again but it was not known if further actions were planned on Monday.
"We will continue our effort to protect the Diaoyus and to retake the Diaoyus," Taiwan organiser Chin Chieh-shou told state radio.
"We will not quit until we succeed."
Shipboard observers said the landing party had tried to reach a controversial lighthouse built in July by a Japanese rightist group, but it was not known if they succeeded.
The activists had vowed to remove Japan's national flag and the lighthouse, whose presence have sparked two months of anti-Japanese protests among Chinese in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and China.

Japan tried to repulse the landing by positioning its patrol boats between the protest fleet and the islands, which it has claimed since 1895 as the Senkakus. Taiwan and China, calling them the Diaoyus, say they have been Chinese for centuries.
"It was very difficult to break through the Japanese ship cordon as the ships tried to collide with us, but we did it," a Taiwan state radio reporter said.
The captain of one protest boat said a Japanese patrol boat had butted his stern, causing minor damage.
Japan's maritime safety agency denied the report.
Taiwan maritime police vessels were in the vicinity to help with rescues if necessary, but were not reported to have intervened in the confrontations.
The operation was the biggest and best-organised in a series of unofficial attempts to claim the islands back from Tokyo by putting Chinese ashore.
The last landing attempt ended in tragedy on September 26, when Hong Kong activists leapt into a a stormy East China Sea to assert China's claim to the islands' waters. Leader David Chan drowned.
Before Monday's attempt, activists had drilled for nearly a week on Taiwan, using motorised rubber rafts and motorcycle-like wave-runners to learn how to mount an amphibious landing.
